blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Digital health – defined broadly as the systematic application of information and communications technologies (ICT), computer science and data 
to support informed decision-making by individuals, the health workforce and health systems, to strengthen resilience to disease and improve health 
and wellness (1) – is increasingly being applied as an essential enabler for health service delivery and accountability. Ministries of health (MOHs) have 
recognized the value of digital health as articulated within the World Health Assembly resolution (2) and the Global strategy on digital health (3). 
Li

summary.text: Explains the background to WHO digital adaptation kits, noting that despite investment in digital health, the data and logic in digital tools are often opaque, inconsistent or proprietary and not clearly linked to evidence-based recommendations. It describes the kits as software-neutral, standardised documentation that distils WHO guidance into content for digital tracking and decision-support systems, mapped to standard terminologies such as ICD. It defines digital tracking and decision support and identifies the core WHO family planning guidance documents the kit draws on, such as the medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use.

blocks.title: Objectives
blocks.content:
This DAK focuses on family planning and aims to provide a common language across various audiences – family planning and other programme 
managers, software developers, and implementers of digital systems – to ensure a common understanding of the appropriate health information content 
within a defined health programme area, as a mechanism to catalyse the effective use of these digital systems. The key objectives of the DAK are:
	»
to ensure adherence to WHO clinical, public health and data use guidelines, and facilitate consistency of the health content that is used to inform 
the development

summary.text: States the objectives of the family planning digital adaptation kit: to keep digital tracking and decision-support systems consistent with WHO guidelines, give health and digital teams a shared understanding of content, and supply core data elements and decision logic. It lists the source guidelines, notes that outputs are generic and must be adapted locally, and mentions related kits for antenatal care, HIV and STIs.

blocks.title: Components of a digital adaptation kit
blocks.content:
The DAK comprises eight interlinked components: (1) health interventions and associated recommendations; (2) generic personas; (3) user scenarios; 
(4) business processes and workflows; (5) core data elements; (6) decision-support logic; (7) indicators and performance metrics; and (8) high-level 
functional and non-functional requirements. Table 1 provides an overview of each of the contributing components of the DAK, which this document 
elaborates. All information within the adaptation kit represents a generic starting point, which can then be adapted according to the specific context.

summary.text: Describes the eight interlinked components of a digital adaptation kit, from health interventions and recommendations, personas and user scenarios through workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and system requirements. A table sets out each component's purpose, outputs and adaptation needs. It also explains the identifier conventions used for data elements, decision tables, indicators and requirements.

blocks.title: How to use this digital adaptation kit
blocks.content:
Target audience
The primary target audience for this DAK is health programme managers within the MOH, who will be working with their digital or health information 
systems counterparts in determining the health content requirements for a family planning DTDS system. The health programme manager is responsible 
for overseeing and monitoring the implementation of the clinical practices and policies for the health programme area, in this case family planning. 
Other stakeholders, including software development teams and implementers in the private sector, will can also benefit from the content in

summary.text: Identifies ministry of health family planning programme managers as the main audience for the kit, working with digital health and information system counterparts and business analysts. It explains how the kit supports collaboration and adaptation to local contexts and notes that client-facing digital tools will be covered in a forthcoming self-care kit.

blocks.title: Generic personas
blocks.content:

the health systems surveyed for this DAK, the common combination of service providers was a lay health worker along with a nurse who was also trained 
as a midwife. The key competences of nurse midwives compared with those of lay health workers are defined by WHO (Table 2 ) (20).
